readall_conflicts: The catalog's antepenultimate rule for Parnkalla (src gordon) rests, as far as the material held by the project shows, on Schürmann 1844 (already saved from the 2026-09-16 pass at, printed p. 2, NLA scanned block p019): 'The accentation of words is subject to nearly the same rules as in the English language; dissyllables have the accent on penultima, in words of three or more syllables, it rests on antipenultima; as: kátta, club, márniti, good, wayandata. The latter of these rules however is not observed in the conjugation of verbs which are apt to retain the accent on the first or second syllable of the root, even when followed by more than two syllables; as ngukaintyanna, ngukaintyaranna.' Two later sources disagree with antepenult for longer words: Hercus 1999 (this task) says initial accent holds in Wirangu 'as is the case in all the surrounding languages' (p. 35), and O'Grady 2001 (also held by the project, p. 292, describing Hale's March 1960 Parnkalla and Karlamayi field notes from Harry Croft at Iron Knob) says 'Stress is usually marked and is invariably on the first syllable.' So the 1844 missionary grammar (nouns antepenult, verbs root-initial) stands against a 1960 direct field record (invariably initial) and a 1999 areal generalization (initial); the three agree on 2- and 3-syllable words and differ only on words of four or more syllables (Schürmann's wayándata vs an initial-stress prediction). The Zuckermann 2019 Barngarla revival booklets held by the project sa…

sources.note: Closest related, fully described Thura-Yura neighbour (initial stress); Clendon 2015:10 cites it for Barngarla dialectology. Would let the catalog annotate the StressTyp coder's flag that antepenultimate stress is areally anomalous and that Schuermann's 3-syllable examples (kátta, márniti) are equally consistent with initial stress -- only wayándata and the verb forms discriminate.

sources.citation: Clendon, Mark (2015 [1844]). Clamor Schürmann's Barngarla grammar. Adelaide: University of Adelaide Press. 201 pp.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.locator: p. 18 (printed), Section 2.3 Vowels; Chapter 2 'Writing Barngarla sounds' pp. 13-20 covers 2.1 Consonants, 2.2 Rhotics, 2.3 Vowels, 2.4 Sandhi only
sources.note: No statement of word stress, accent or tone anywhere in the book: a full-text search for stress/stressed/accent/tone/prosody/pitch/intonation/rhythm/prominence/suprasegmental returns nothing (the only 'tone' hits are 'stone'). The phonology chapter (pp. 13-20) treats the consonant inventory, prestopping of non-velar nasals and laterals 'at the start of the second syllable in a word' (p. 13), the rhotic contrast, the four-vowel system with long aa, vowel harmony, and vowel sandhi; syllable count is mentioned only for root/word shapes. Vowel length is phonemic (long aa) but is not tied to stress
